title: MCP 2026-07-28: The Stateless Spec Revision
content:
## Overview

On July 28, 2026, the Model Context Protocol maintainers finalized the **2026-07-28 specification revision** — the largest change to MCP since it launched in November 2024. The headline change: MCP drops its stateful session model entirely in favor of a stateless core, and moves several features out of the base spec into an opt-in Extensions framework.

---

## Why Statelessness

The original MCP design required a handshake and a session ID, which in production forced every serious deployment to run sticky load-balancer routing, a shared session store (commonly Redis), and deep packet inspection at the gateway just to route a request to the right server instance.

Under the 2026-07-28 revision:

- **No handshake, no session ID.** Any request can hit any server instance.
- Servers can run behind a **plain round-robin load balancer** — no sticky sessions required.
- Clients can route on the `Mcp-Method` header instead of inspecting request bodies.
- Clients may cache `tools/list` responses for as long as the server's `ttlMs` value permits, cutting redundant round-trips.

This lets MCP servers scale on ordinary HTTP infrastructure the same way a typical REST API does.

---

## Extensions Framework

Features that used to live in the core spec now ship as formally versioned **extensions** that clients and servers can opt into independently:

### Tasks Extension
Tasks shipped as an experimental core feature in the 2025-11-25 revision, but production use surfaced enough required redesign that the maintainers moved it to an extension rather than keep iterating on it inside the core spec. Under the stateless model, a server answers `tools/call` with a task handle, and the client drives progress with `tasks/get`, `tasks/update`, and `tasks/cancel` — enabling long-running operations (e.g., a multi-minute data export) without holding a session open.

### MCP Apps Extension (SEP-1865)
Lets servers ship interactive HTML interfaces that hosts render inside a sandboxed iframe. Tools declare their UI templates ahead of time, so hosts can prefetch, cache, and security-review the UI before it ever executes. Crucially, the rendered UI talks back to the host over the *same* JSON-RPC base protocol used for everything else in MCP — so a button click inside a rendered MCP App goes through the identical audit and consent path as a direct tool call, rather than opening a side channel.

### Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA)
Promoted to stable status earlier in July 2026. Gives organizations a centralized way to control access to MCP servers through their existing identity provider, aligning MCP's auth model more closely with standard OAuth 2.1 / OpenID Connect enterprise deployments.

---

## Compatibility

- Deprecated features remain functional for **at least 12 months** under a new formal deprecation policy — the first time MCP has committed to a concrete compatibility window.
- This is not a blanket interoperability guarantee: **servers built on 2026-07-28 may not work with older (pre-stateless) clients, and vice versa.** Teams running MCP servers in production should check both client and server revision support before upgrading.

---

## Why It Matters

MCP had already become the de facto standard for connecting models to external tools — by mid-2026 estimates put the number of public MCP servers above 10,000. This revision addresses the operational pain points (session affinity, scaling, auth) that were the main friction points for running MCP servers at enterprise scale, rather than adding new model-facing capabilities. Combined with MCP Apps, it also opens the door to richer, UI-bearing tool responses instead of plain text/JSON tool results.

For Claude Code and other MCP clients, this means: server authors can simplify their infrastructure, tool-list caching should reduce latency on repeated sessions, and any custom MCP server relying on session-scoped state will need to be re-architected around the Tasks extension or explicit state passed in each request.
